name: Cost Projection Model
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Forecasting a Bill That Won't Sit Still
lesson.summary: A cost projection model extends a total-cost-of-ownership snapshot into a forward-looking estimate of how blockchain costs will change over time, under explicit assumptions about transaction volume, fee markets, and protocol changes.
lesson.body:
A total cost of ownership figure, as developed in the previous section, is a snapshot: what the system costs right now, given current transaction volume and current fees. A cost projection model takes that snapshot and extends it forward, estimating how capital and operating expenses are likely to change over the system's planned lifetime, under a stated set of assumptions. The point is not to predict the future precisely, which is not really possible for a system with as many volatile inputs as a public blockchain, but to make the assumptions driving a cost forecast explicit enough that they can be checked, debated, and updated as conditions change.

A blockchain cost projection has to model several moving parts at once. Transaction volume is one axis: as adoption grows, the number of on-chain operations a system performs each month generally rises, and that rise is not necessarily linear if the underlying business is growing exponentially or seasonally. Fee market behavior is a second, harder axis: on Ethereum, for example, the fee mechanism introduced by EIP-1559 in 2021 replaced a simple first-price auction with a base fee that adjusts block by block based on demand, plus an optional tip to validators, with a portion of the base fee burned rather than paid to anyone; a projection model built before that change would have badly mispredicted costs afterward, which is the general risk with any model that assumes today's fee mechanism holds indefinitely. Node and infrastructure costs are a third axis, since growing chain state generally raises the hardware requirements to run a full node over time.

One of the trickier realities a good projection model has to capture is that blockchain costs do not scale smoothly with usage. Because block space is a fixed, auctioned resource, costs can behave close to linearly at moderate demand and then rise sharply once the network approaches capacity, because every additional transaction is now bidding against every other pending transaction for the same limited block space. A projection model that assumes cost per transaction stays constant as volume grows will understate costs precisely during the periods, like a popular application launch or a market event, when accurate cost forecasting matters most.

Because so many of these inputs are uncertain, a defensible cost projection model presents a range tied to explicit scenarios rather than a single number: a low-growth case, an expected case, and a high-congestion case, each with its own assumptions about transaction volume and fee levels stated up front. Protocol upgrades are a further wrinkle specific to blockchain systems: a network's governance process, whether on-chain or off-chain as covered earlier in this chapter, can change the fee mechanism, block size, or consensus rules in ways that shift the cost structure the model was built around, so a serious projection should flag which of its assumptions are exposed to a plausible future governance decision.

A single projection, even a scenario-based one, still only samples a handful of possible futures. The next section builds on this model by running many randomized variations of these assumptions to see the full distribution of likely outcomes, rather than just a few hand-picked cases.
